summary: Specifies version 2 of Multicast Listener Discovery, used by IPv6 routers to learn which multicast addresses neighbors want. MLDv2 lets a node ask for traffic from specific sources, or from all except some. It updates RFC 2710, was updated by RFC 4604, and was replaced by RFC 9777.

eli5.summary: A router asks, who here wants this channel? MLDv2 lets listeners also say, only from this sender, or anyone but that one.

questions: how does mld source filtering work
what is the difference between mldv1 and mldv2
subtitle: How IPv6 routers learn which multicast groups, and which senders, their neighbors want to hear.

tldr.problem: An IPv6 router must know which multicast addresses have listeners on each attached link. MLDv1 could not say which senders a listener wanted or did not want.
tldr.mechanism: MLDv2 has the router (the Querier) ask for listening state, and nodes answer with reports. Each report carries a filter mode, INCLUDE or EXCLUDE, and a source list, so a node can ask for traffic only from some sources or from all but some.
tldr.outcome: This Proposed Standard updates RFC 2710, was updated by RFC 4604, and has been obsoleted by RFC 9777.

today: RFC 3810 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 2710. It was updated by RFC 4604 and has since been obsoleted by RFC 9777.

sections.title: What MLDv2 Does
sections.content:
Multicast Listener Discovery (MLD) is used by IPv6 routers to discover multicast listeners on their directly attached links, and to learn which multicast addresses are of interest. MLDv2 is a translation of IGMPv3 to IPv6 semantics, and it is designed to interoperate with MLDv1.

The new feature is source filtering: a node can report that it wants packets for a multicast address only from specific sources, or from all but specific sources. This is what Source-Specific Multicast needs.

MLD is asymmetric. Listeners (hosts or routers) run the listener part of the protocol, and multicast routers run the router part on each attached link. A router only needs to know that at least one node on a link wants a given address and source, not what each neighbor wants.
sections.eli5: Routers need to know who is listening so they only send traffic where someone wants it. MLDv2 adds the chance to say which senders you trust or want.

sections.title: Filter Modes and Listening State
sections.content:
Listening state is a set of records, each holding a multicast address, a filter mode and a source list. In INCLUDE mode, reception is enabled only from the listed sources. In EXCLUDE mode it is enabled from all sources except the listed ones. Applications call a service interface, IPv6MulticastListen, with a socket, interface, address, filter mode and source list. Start Listening is equivalent to EXCLUDE with an empty list, and Stop Listening is INCLUDE with an empty list.

A node keeps per-socket state and derives per-interface state from it. If all sockets are INCLUDE, the interface list is the union of their lists. If any socket is EXCLUDE, the interface list is the intersection of the EXCLUDE lists minus any sources in INCLUDE records. For example, sockets with EXCLUDE {a,b,c,d}, EXCLUDE {b,c,d,e} and INCLUDE {d,e,f} give an interface record of EXCLUDE {b,c}.

Routers keep similar state per address per link: a filter mode, a source list and timers. A router is in INCLUDE mode when all listeners are INCLUDE, and in EXCLUDE mode when at least one listener uses EXCLUDE.
sections.eli5: Each listener hands in either a want list (only these senders) or a block list (everyone except these). The router merges the lists so everybody gets what they asked for.

sections.title: Queries and Reports
sections.content:
MLDv2 is a sub-protocol of ICMPv6, identified by a Next Header value of 58. Every message MUST have a link-local source address, an IPv6 Hop Limit of 1 and a Router Alert option in a Hop-by-Hop Options header. Two message types matter: the Multicast Listener Query (type 130) and the Version 2 Multicast Listener Report (type 143). Implementations also handle MLDv1 Report (131) and Done (132).

There are three query variants. A General Query asks which addresses have listeners and is sent to FF02::1. A Multicast Address Specific Query asks about one address. A Multicast Address and Source Specific Query asks about specific sources for one address. The Maximum Response Code sets how long nodes may wait before replying, the S flag tells other routers to suppress timer updates, and the QRV and QQIC fields carry the Querier's robustness variable and query interval.

Reports go to FF02:0:0:0:0:0:0:16, the address of all MLDv2-capable routers, and hold Multicast Address Records. The six record types report either the current state or a change.
sections.eli5: The router sends out a question, and listeners write back answers on a form. The form says which channel and which senders they want or do not want.

sections.title: How Listeners and Routers Behave
sections.content:
When a node's listening state changes, it sends a State Change Report immediately. To survive packet loss it retransmits, with ([Robustness Variable] - 1) retransmissions at random intervals. The Robustness Variable defaults to 2. When a Query arrives, a node does not reply at once. It waits a random time up to the Maximum Response Delay and combines pending responses.

Routers elect one Querier per link. A router starts out assuming it is the Querier, and a router that hears a Query from a lower IPv6 address stops querying. The Querier sends periodic General Queries (default Query Interval is 125 seconds). When it sees a report that a node stopped listening to an address or source, it first sends a specific query to check for other listeners before it stops forwarding, which gives a fast leave. Last Listener Query Interval defaults to 1 second.

Router state per source is tracked with timers. The Multicast Address Listening Interval is the Robustness Variable times the Query Interval plus the Query Response Interval. MLDv2 only suggests forwarding to the routing protocol and does not override it.
sections.eli5: One router per street does the asking. If someone says they are leaving, it double-checks nobody else still wants the channel before it shuts it off.

sections.title: Working with MLDv1
sections.content:
MLDv2 nodes interoperate with MLDv1 devices. A Query of exactly 24 octets is MLDv1, and one of 28 octets or more is MLDv2; other lengths MUST be silently ignored. A host that hears an MLDv1 Query switches that interface to MLDv1 compatibility mode and uses only MLDv1 until the Older Version Querier Present timer runs out.

Routers keep a compatibility mode per multicast address. When an MLDv1 Report arrives for an address, the router treats it as MLDv1 for that address and translates the Report to IS_EX({}) and the Done message to TO_IN({}). Source-list information in BLOCK and TO_EX messages is then ignored for that address. If an MLDv1 router is on the link, the administrator must configure MLDv2 routers to act in MLDv1 mode, and the Querier then sends 24-byte General Queries.
sections.eli5: Old devices only know the simple version of the question. New devices notice this and speak the old way when needed, then switch back when the old device goes quiet.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Before processing a message, a node checks that the source address is link-local (or unspecified for Reports), that the Hop Limit is 1 and that the Router Alert option is present. This protects against forged messages from off-link, so the RFC only discusses on-link forgery.

A forged Query from a lower address can make the forger the Querier. A forged Version 1 Query or Report can push listeners or routers into MLDv1 mode, so source filtering stops working. The RFC suggests a configuration option to ignore Version 1 messages entirely, which breaks automatic compatibility and should only be used where source filtering is critical. Forged Multicast Address and Source Specific Queries could be used for a denial-of-service attack by making a node store many sources, so implementations could limit the queries per address and the number of sources recorded.

A forged State Change Report only causes extra queries and cannot cause desired traffic to be lost.
sections.eli5: Someone on the same street could pretend to be the router or send fake answers. The rules make it hard to fake from far away, but nearby tricks are still possible.

fields.name: Code
fields.desc: Zero from the sender; ignored by receivers.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: Standard ICMPv6 checksum over the whole message.

fields.name: Maximum Response Code
fields.desc: Maximum time allowed before a responding Report is sent.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Zero from the sender; ignored by receivers.

fields.name: Multicast Address
fields.desc: Zero for a General Query; the queried address otherwise.
